analysis.investment_thesis: Neogen Chemicals trades at INR 1,512 — roughly 5x my calculated Graham Number of ~INR 301 (sqrt(22.5 × EPS₁₃.₃ × BVPS₃₀₃)) — offering zero margin of safety. The business is being strangled by its own debt load, with finance costs consuming an ever-larger share of earnings while free cash flow has been negative every single year for five years.
key_strengths: Nine consecutive years of positive net profit (2016–2025) — passes my earnings continuity test
Revenue CAGR of 25.6% over nine years demonstrates genuine end-market demand across pharma, agro, and battery sectors
Gross margin of 45.85% signals a real specialty franchise, not a commodity processor
key_risks: Borrowings exploded from INR 409 Cr to INR 1,132 Cr in a single year (FY25) — D/E now 1.41 vs my ceiling of 0.5; the company is dangerously leveraged
Interest coverage of only 2.8x (EBIT INR 136 Cr ÷ finance cost INR 48 Cr) falls below my 3.5x minimum — one bad year destroys debt-service capacity
Net profit has declined from INR 50 Cr (FY23) to INR 35 Cr (FY25) even as revenue grew 13% — finance costs are eating the business alive
red_flags: P/E of 150 is 10× my maximum threshold of 15 — the price contains a decade of speculative hope, not proven earning power
P/B of 4.98 is 3.3× my ceiling of 1.5 — you are paying INR 5 for every INR 1 of net assets
Free cash flow negative in every year from 2020–2025 (FY25 FCF: –INR 121 Cr) — this company has never converted profits to cash
Cash on hand collapsed to INR 5 Cr in FY25 against total debt of INR 597+ Cr — near-zero liquidity cushion
Other income swung from +INR 8 Cr (FY24) to –INR 10 Cr (FY25) — unexplained reversal warrants scrutiny
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Neogen fails every quantitative filter I apply. The Graham Number — my bedrock of intrinsic value based on proven earning power and net assets — stands at approximately INR 301, implying the stock must fall 80% just to reach fair value. A P/E of 150 and P/B of 5.0 tell me that Mr. Market has priced in a brilliant future that the financial statements do not yet justify. The company earned only INR 35 Cr on a market capitalisation of nearly INR 4,000 Cr — an earnings yield of less than 1%. I require at minimum a 6–7% earnings yield before I even begin to negotiate.

The balance sheet has deteriorated sharply. Borrowings tripled in a single year to INR 1,132 Cr, and the cash pile has been reduced to an alarming INR 5 Cr. Capital expenditure is running at INR 317–318 Cr per year — entirely funded by debt — with INR 335 Cr still sitting in capital work-in-progress. Until these projects come onstream and begin generating cash, the company is essentially a leveraged bet on future capacity. That is speculation, not investment. The intelligent investor demands that he be paid to wait; here, the price demands that you pay dearly for the privilege of waiting.
